claims.text: Equiatomic FeCoNi has an FCC structure.
FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization and low coercivity.
The proposed intervention produces equiatomic or nearly equiatomic FeCoNiCr.
Equiatomic FeCoNiCr has configurational entropy of at least 1.0R.
Introducing Cr into FeCoNi will increase coercivity relative to FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt.
Controlled thermal and solidification processing can produce a homogeneous FeCoNiCr high-entropy structure.
Cr substitution is expected to increase lattice distortion in FeCoNiCr.
Cr substitution may promote an FCC structure containing minor BCC or ordered nanoprecipitate phases.
A secondary phase in FeCoNiCr would act as a barrier to magnetic domain-wall motion.
Cr has antiferromagnetic tendencies relative to Fe, Co, and Ni.
Cr-induced lattice strain and local chemical ordering can enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Increased anisotropy and minor hard-magnetic features impede domain-wall motion.
Impeded domain-wall motion raises coercivity.
FeCoNiCr may have coercivity several times that of FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt.
FeCoNiCr will retain acceptable saturation magnetization after Cr addition.
FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt are soft ferromagnets with low coercivity.
Excessive Cr or phase segregation may substantially reduce saturation magnetization.
The intervention is expected to work only while nearly equiatomic mixing and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R are maintained.
The coercivity enhancement and saturation-magnetization trade-off depend sensitively on secondary-phase fraction, secondary-phase distribution, and processing conditions.
A coercivity increase greater than 50% relative to a similarly processed FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt control is the proposed success threshold.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes Cr as substituting for one original FeCoNi constituent, but the stated product retains Fe, Co, and Ni and adds Cr as a fourth equiatomic element. Replacing one constituent would ordinarily yield a ternary alloy rather than equiatomic FeCoNiCr.
